transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~72m | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood Platform), Dr. Lena Park (Sterling Eng Lead), Tom Whitaker (Sterling SRE), Aisha Mohammed (Sterling PM)
Summary: Deep dive on prompt-index signatures, hotset/hot-key detection for KV/prompt cache, multi-tenant safety and eviction policy tradeoffs. Discussed hit-rate telemetry, tenant isolation, quantization impacts on latency, and VPC/on-prem pilot constraints. Agreed on telemetry export and on-prem microbench next steps.
Topics: hotset detection, cache key design, prefix normalization, tenant-level quotas, eviction policies, batching strategies, 4-bit quantization tradeoffs, VPC pilot constraints (KMS, SAML, audit logs).

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we will jump into the heatmap you sent, Lena.
[00:14] Dr. Lena Park: Hi all, thanks. We wanna make sure the cache doesn't leak across tenants, and our tail latency goal is 95th percentile under 250ms for chat paths.
[00:26] Tom Whitaker: And SRE wants predictable p95 as well, also need to understand how batching will affect our bursty traffic.
[00:38] Priya Kapoor: Great — we'll walk through prefix indexing and our hotset approach. Marco will chime in on eviction heuristics. Couple of caveats: some of our terms get transcribed funny, so "K-V cash" might show up as "k-v cash" in notes.
[00:52] Marco Ruiz: Also for context, Redwood's runtime supports per-tenant key partitioning and optional strict isolation where prefixes never overlap unless explicitly aliased.

[01:15] Dr. Lena Park: You mentioned prefix normalization. We have a bunch of prompts with user metadata (timestamps, ids) so normalization is key. How aggressive is normalization out-of-the-box?
[01:29] Priya Kapoor: By default we strip PII-like tokens if you enable the prompt transform pipeline; normalization rules are regex and token-aware. We recommend a two-level key: (1) signature of normalized prompt, (2) tenant id. So the cache key is effectively tenant:signature. That prevents cross-tenant sharing.
[01:50] Tom Whitaker: Does that still allow shared hot keys if two tenants deliberately use the same prompt? We're not comfortable with cross-tenant mixing.
[02:02] Alex Chen: We have a policy mode "strict-silo" where tenant is always part of the key and cache entries are never returned across tenants. There's also a "shared-hotset" mode for customers who opt-in to share certain prompt families for cost efficiency.
[02:17] Aisha Mohammed: Our product team will not opt-in to sharing. We need strong guarantees.

[02:40] Priya Kapoor: Ok, strict-silo then. For hit-rate telemetry, can you show the heatmap you exported?
[02:48] Dr. Lena Park: Sure — I pasted a link earlier: https://sterling-analytics.s3/metrics/hotset-2025-06.csv (shared in the chat). The file is a CSV with prefix signature, count, tenant id, last seen timestamp.
[03:05] Priya Kapoor: Reviewing... looks like a classic long tail. Top ~0.8% of signatures account for 42% of requests, but the distribution varies significantly across your tenants. Some tenants have very concentrated hotsets, others much flatter.
[03:25] Tom Whitaker: Important context: a small set of tenants (finance-sandbox, test-team) produce very high chattiness. We can move them to dedicated capacity if needed.

[03:45] Marco Ruiz: For eviction policies we suggested an LRU with hot-extension and a weighted TTL that factors in token-length cost and recency. So if a prefix is short but very frequent we keep it longer.
[04:00] Dr. Lena Park: Weighted TTL sounds good. How do you compute weight?
[04:06] Priya Kapoor: Weight = alpha * frequency + beta * recencyScore + gamma * tenantPriority. We can tune alphas per-tenant; by default alpha=0.7, beta=0.2, gamma=0.1.
[04:20] Dr. Lena Park: Could you export that formula? We need to audit the math.
[04:26] Alex Chen: We'll include the formula and a sample calc in the telemetry template.

[05:00] [05:00] Aisha Mohammed: Clarify the KV cache itself — are we storing embeddings or raw prompt prefixes?
[05:08] Priya Kapoor: Good question. The Redwood prefix cache stores the normalized prompt tokens and the model KV (Key/Value) state needed to resume generation. We do not store full user embeddings by default unless you enable a separate embedding cache. The prefix cache is model-specific; it's keyed by model-version + prefix signature + tenant id in strict-silo.
[05:28] Tom Whitaker: What's the typical size per entry? We need to estimate memory for the VPC pilot.
[05:34] Marco Ruiz: It depends on sequence length and kv compression. For a 2k-context model, a full KV for a prefix with 512 tokens is roughly 4–8MB in 16-bit, and ~1.2MB in 4-bit with quantization-friendly kernel paths — caveat: quantized KV sizes vary by implementation.
[05:56] Dr. Lena Park: Wait you said 1.2MB in 4-bit. Is that with Redwood's Q4_0 style packing or a different scheme?
[06:03] Priya Kapoor: It's our internal q4-repack with packing and reindexing; microbench results vary but generally you see ~3–6x reduction vs fp16. We'll share the microbench.

[06:30] Alex Chen: On quantization and latency — two tradeoffs: memory footprint and compute path. In some cases 4-bit quant reduces memory enough to fit more hotsets in GPU, reducing offload and improving p95, but quantization can slightly increase per-token compute depending on kernel availability.
[06:53] Tom Whitaker: So we should benchmark our 95th latency on our typical prompt mix.
[06:58] Priya Kapoor: Exactly — Priya (smiles) will run a 4k token synthetic microbench on a node similar to your VPC pilot and share tail-latency graphs.

[07:12] Dr. Lena Park: Concurrency — what's batching behavior for chat? We have many short chats with immediate responses.
[07:20] Marco Ruiz: Redwood runtime supports dynamic batching with an upper bound latency SLO per route. For chat short-turns we use mini-batching (50–200ms window) and prioritized batching for low-latency routes. You can configure route-level batch windows and max batch sizes.
[07:35] Tom Whitaker: If we set batch window to 50ms, will that increase p50 but hurt p99?
[07:41] Priya Kapoor: It can reduce cost significantly while keeping p95 within target if traffic has moderate concurrency. For extremely spiky traffic, set smaller windows and enable burst capacity. We also support token-aware batching where initial tokens are prioritized for latency.

[08:10] [08:10] Dr. Lena Park: Another vector — tenant isolation for cached entries in memory shared across GPUs. Are there cross-tenant side-channels we're concerned about?
[08:20] Marco Ruiz: We design isolation both at key-level and memory-region level. With strict-silo keys you avoid logical sharing. For customers requiring extra protection, we offer tenant-dedicated pools where nothing else runs on the same GPU. That addresses both data residency and side-channel concerns.
[08:39] Dr. Lena Park: Dedication is attractive but expensive. Are there mitigations short of dedicating GPUs?
[08:46] Alex Chen: Yes — scheduled scramble windows, per-tenant namespace randomization, and periodic zeroing of memory pages when evicting entries. Not perfect against advanced side-channel attacks but closes most practical risks. We'll provide the security spec.

[09:10] Aisha Mohammed: On the VPC/on-prem side: KMS integration and SSO are must-haves. How do you manage keys?
[09:19] Priya Kapoor: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp Vault). On private deployments we support HSM-based key wraps and do audit logs for decryption events. We'll need your security team to sign the connector docs.
[09:34] Tom Whitaker: We use SAML SSO and already have an audit pipeline. Can Redwood push signed audit events into our S3 or a syslog endpoint?
[09:42] Marco Ruiz: Yes — audit hooks can forward to S3, Pub/Sub, or syslog. We also integrate with SIEMs for alerting.

[10:10] [10:10] Dr. Lena Park: Back to hit rate: our CSV shows some prefixes with extremely long tail reuses separated by hours. How do you tune TTLs for such patterns?
[10:20] Priya Kapoor: For long-tail reuses we have two substrategies: (1) cold-shelf storage — evicted entries go to a compressed s3-backed object that can be rehydrated slowly; (2) Bloom-filter guided re-insertion — if a prefix is reaccessed within X hours it gets a weighted bump. Cold-shelf for Sterling could reduce memory load by ~18% while still keeping rehydration latency acceptable for non-interactive flows.
[10:48] Tom Whitaker: Rehydration is fine for some batch summaries but not for chat.
[10:53] Priya Kapoor: Right — we'll suggest classifying routes: interactive chat vs background generation. Interactive routes keep hot prefixes in-memory; background can use cold-shelf.

[11:12] Alex Chen: Quick note about key synthesis: sometimes customers canonicalize prompts with stable templating so prefix signatures are stable; other times users add small randomness which fragments the hotset. We recommended a deterministic hashing after template application.
[11:30] Dr. Lena Park: We do have user-injected randomness in a few analytic prompts for trace IDs. We'll need to put a sanitizer to strip them before signature.
[11:40] Priya Kapoor: Yes, put the sanitizer early in the pipeline. We can share a sample sanitizer script.

[12:05] [12:05] Aisha Mohammed: Let's talk about safety: rate limiting combined with cache eviction — if we evict aggressively a tenant might hit recompute storms. How do you prevent rebuild storms?
[12:18] Marco Ruiz: We use jittered backoff on rehydration and a write-through warm strategy. If an entry is evicted and then requested, the first request triggers a warm write; subsequent parallel requests can multiplex on the inflight load to avoid multiple simultaneous recomputes.
[12:36] Tom Whitaker: How long is the multiplex window?
[12:39] Priya Kapoor: Configurable — default 200ms for typical workloads, up to 1s for heavier generation workloads.

[13:00] [13:00] Dr. Lena Park: On observability: we want per-tenant hit-rate, per-signature latency, and eviction reasons logged. Can Redwood produce those metrics at 1m granularity?
[13:13] Marco Ruiz: We can. The default retention is 30 days, and we can push raw telemetry to your S3 for longer retention. We'll provide a pre-baked dashboard you can import into Grafana.

[13:40] Alex Chen: I want to flag one more tradeoff: using shared hotset pooling across tenants lowers cost but increases blast radius. Since Sterling won't opt-in to sharing, we can focus on strict-silo + per-tenant quotas and optional dedicated pools for the noisy tenants.
[13:58] Aisha Mohammed: Sounds good. We'll identify noisy tenants.

[14:20] [14:20] Dr. Lena Park: Let's cover quantization a bit more — do we lose cache compatibility across quantization configs? If we change from q4 to q2 or fp16, is cached KV invalidated?
[14:33] Priya Kapoor: Cache entries are tied to model-config fingerprint (architecture + quantization format + model weights checksum). Changing quant config or model version creates a new namespace so old KVs are not reused. We provide cross-quant warmup scripts but not automatic reuse.
[14:52] Tom Whitaker: That means rolling quantization changes will cause cold-starts for everyone.
[14:56] Marco Ruiz: We mitigate via staged rollouts, canary nodes, and background prewarm of top N prefixes. We'll propose a canary plan.

[15:20] [15:20] Dr. Lena Park: For the on-prem option, how heavy is the install footprint? We have limited rack space for pilot.
[15:28] Marco Ruiz: Pilot for a single dedicated pool: one 8-GPU box (A100/RTX equivalent), 256GB RAM, NVMe for cold-shelf, plus a small control VM. If you don't want ded- hardware, Redwood Dedicated in cloud could be used for the pilot.
[15:45] Aisha Mohammed: Price aside, rack density is the constraint.

[16:05] Alex Chen: Now performance numbers — Priya, can you call out the microbench numbers you expect to share?
[16:12] Priya Kapoor: We'll run: p50/p95/p99 for interactive chat at 1, 4, 8 concurrent streams with and without q4 quantization, plus KV cache hit vs miss latencies and memory per entry. Expect a small increase in per-token for q4 in some kernels but net win due to less offload.

[16:40] [16:40] Tom Whitaker: Security — you mentioned zeroing memory pages on eviction. Is that a synchronous zero or deferred?
[16:48] Marco Ruiz: Deferred zeroing with guaranteed periodic scrub; we can enable synchronous zeroing if your security team insists but it has a CPU overhead. We'll document the options.

[17:10] Dr. Lena Park: A few quick objections from my team: (1) we worry about prefix-norm false positives; (2) we're concerned about tenant churn causing frequent eviction; (3) the complexity of key derivation might break debugging.
[17:26] Priya Kapoor: For (1) we provide a signature collision report and collision-resilient hashing; (2) eviction pressure can be handled via tenant quotas/priority and quota-based autoscaling; (3) we expose the key derivation pipeline as part of the logs so you can map request -> signature.

[18:00] [18:00] Alex Chen: Recap: strict-silo cache keys, per-tenant quotas, cold-shelf for non-interactive flows, multiplexed rehydrate to avoid rebuild storms, on-prem pilot sizing and quantized microbench.

[18:20] Aisha Mohammed: Any notes on licensing or contract clauses around data retention?
[18:26] Alex Chen: We'll share the enterprise addendum covering retention, audit logs, SOC2 controls, and KMS responsibilities.

[18:40] [18:40] Dr. Lena Park: Great. For the next steps: we'll extract top-100 prefixes and share sample traffic; Redwood will provide telemetry template and microbench results.

[19:00] [19:00] (wrap-up) Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifact links and a short 30-min canary planning session.
